results.name: trial_index_yes_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on trial_index (per 100 trials); observed > model means people drift toward saying "yes" more as the session goes on, which the trial-invariant model cannot produce, observed < model means a drift toward "no".

results.name: parity_mismatch_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity, the yes-rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed > model means people use parity less strictly (generalize across parity more) than the model predicts, observed < model means they reject parity violators more sharply.
results.code:
# name: parity_mismatch_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity, the yes-rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed > model means people use parity less strictly (generalize across parity more) than the model predicts, observed < model means they reject parity violators more sharply.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(ex), 2), np.nan)
    allodd = (np.nansum(par, axis=1) == n)
    alleven = (np.nansum(par, axis=1) == 0)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    m = (n >= 2) & ((allodd & (t % 2 == 0)) | (alleven & (t % 2 == 1)))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)[m].mean())

results.name: four_example_set_mean_sd
results.description: Standard deviation, across four-example sets, of each set's overall yes-rate; observed > model means sets differ in how readily people say "yes" more than the model predicts (model too homogeneous across set types), observed < model means less heterogeneity than predicted.

results.name: same_decade_nonexample_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of 1-2 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets in the same decade (same tens digit, 100 counted with 90s) as some example; observed > model means people generalize to decade-mates after little evidence more than the model predicts, observed < model means less.
results.code:
# name: same_decade_nonexample_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of 1-2 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets in the same decade (same tens digit, 100 counted with 90s) as some example; observed > model means people generalize to decade-mates after little evidence more than the model predicts, observed < model means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dec_e = np.floor(np.minimum(ex, 99) / 10.0)
    dec_t = np.floor(np.minimum(t, 99) / 10.0)[:, None]
    same = (dec_e == dec_t).any(axis=1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = (n <= 2) & same & ~isex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)[m].mean())

results.name: outside_hull_distance_slope
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples and targets outside the examples' min-max range, the OLS slope of yes on distance (in units of 10) to the nearest example; a more negative observed value than the model means people's yes-rate falls off with distance more steeply than predicted (similarity gradient), a less negative/positive one means flatter generalization than predicted.
results.code:
# name: outside_hull_distance_slope
# description: For sets of 2+ examples and targets outside the examples' min-max range, the OLS slope of yes on distance (in units of 10) to the nearest example; a more negative observed value than the model means people's yes-rate falls off with distance more steeply than predicted (similarity gradient), a less negative/positive one means flatter generalization than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = (n >= 2) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if m.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    d = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, t - hi)[m] / 10.0
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)[m]
    dc = d - d.mean()
    v = (dc ** 2).sum()
    if v == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((dc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / v)

results.name: single_example_last_digit_contrast
results.description: For single-example sets, yes-rate on (non-example) targets sharing the example's last digit minus yes-rate on other non-example targets; observed > model means people lean on the "same last digit" rule after one example more than the model's guessing-diluted posterior predicts, observed < model means less.
results.code:
# name: single_example_last_digit_contrast
# description: For single-example sets, yes-rate on (non-example) targets sharing the example's last digit minus yes-rate on other non-example targets; observed > model means people lean on the "same last digit" rule after one example more than the model's guessing-diluted posterior predicts, observed < model means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "-1"), errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    base = single.to_numpy() & (t != e)
    same = base & (t % 10 == e % 10)
    other = base & (t % 10 != e % 10)
    if same.sum() == 0 or other.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[same].mean() - y[other].mean())

results.name: target_is_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed < model means people reject already-shown examples far more often than a concept-membership model (which puts them in nearly every posterior concept) predicts, observed > model means the reverse.

results.name: single_example_within_set_spread
results.description: Mean over single-example sets of the standard deviation (across targets) of per-(set,target) yes-rates; observed > model means people discriminate between targets after one example more sharply than the model's evidence-scarce guessing allows (guessing too flat), observed < model means responses are flatter than predicted.
